Text:
About three years before the account was written, a family could not find a good housemaid. On the way to New York the writer asked to be led to a girl of good character who would value a Christian home. At a boarding-house on Greenwich Street she was told they had a Swede just landed. She spoke through an interpreter and took her.

The girl said several places had been offered that morning, and she had not liked them. As soon as she saw this household she was willing to go. She was a Christian, a member of the Lutheran church, and she wanted a Christian home. In two years of service she was almost faultless.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE ASKED, ON THE WAY TO NEW YORK, FOR A HOUSEMAID WHO WANTED A CHRISTIAN HOME.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Family Pray For A Good Servant."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A boy named Johnnie was diligent at school and found parsing hard. He asked his mother to help him analyze some sentences. She showed him the manner of it. He followed her, and still could not see the reasons for himself. She told him it was hard then, and that after more study it would be easier.

He went into another room. He came back radiant and said he wanted to begin again. He had asked Jesus to help him, and he thought he saw how it was. He said Jesus always helps when we ask. They went over the lesson again.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: PARSING WAS HARD. HE WENT TO ANOTHER ROOM, ASKED, AND CAME BACK READY TO BEGIN AGAIN.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Asking The Lord to Help Him in his Lessons."). Retold here in modern English.

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 34.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: THIS IS THE MESSAGE WHICH WE HAVE HEARD OF THEE
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 34.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
When her husband died, two hundred dollars were due an institute for the board and tuition of their two boys. The principal pressed, and at last was abusive. She cried to the Lord for a week.

A gentleman she had nursed through a dangerous illness three years before stopped to say goodbye. He was bound for a Bremen steamer. His baggage was on board except the valise in his hand. He asked if her boy might ride to the wharf. The boy came back with a letter. It held two hundred dollars, and the words that money could not express his gratitude, but the enclosed might help with gas-bills or some small household matter.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: TWO HUNDRED DOLLARS WERE DUE THE INSTITUTE. HIS BAGGAGE WAS ABOARD. THE LETTER CAME BACK WITH THE BOY.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Two Hundred Dollars Needed and Given at the Last Moment."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 209:

"And now, Lord, what wait we for? Truly our hope is even in thee, and on thee do we depend to be to us a God all-sufficient." Psalm 39:7. Genesis 17:1.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: AND NOW, LORD, WHAT WAIT WE FOR?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 209. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
After three weeks without work he found a place. He pawned his best clothes to move. On Monday morning the cart set them down with ten pence half-penny for himself, his wife, and his child until Saturday night. They asked that relief would be sent as God thought proper.

The next evening the landlord's daughter and son-in-law came to see their mother and brought baked meat just out of the oven, for him and his wife to sup with them. The account says these people knew nothing of them or of their God. They did the same the next evening, and sent victuals and garden stuff all that week.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: TEN PENCE AND A HALFPENNY WERE LEFT UNTIL SATURDAY. THE NEXT EVENING THEY BROUGHT BAKED MEAT.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("God Sent Supplies."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A donor enclosed one hundred dollars to a sister institution and withheld his name. He said he began business hoping to be rich. A year later he became a Christian and adopted Cobb's Resolutions. Four or five years after that he read Normand Smith's Memoir and Wesley's sermon on the use of money, and he devoted his gains to benevolent uses, reserving five thousand dollars while he remained unmarried.

In about sixteen years, he wrote, by the grace of God and nothing else, he had given about twenty-four thousand five hundred dollars, and had lent about five hundred that was not returned.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE WITHHELD HIS NAME AND SENT A HUNDRED. IN SIXTEEN YEARS HE HAD GIVEN ABOUT TWENTY-FOUR THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Another Example Of Beneficence."). Retold here in modern English.

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 35.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: WE CANNOT BY SEARCHING FIND OUT GOD
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 35.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A Christian evangelist told of the days of his folly, when his life ran against his mother's prayers. He asked her whether she really believed he would ever be converted. She said yes: that he would one day be as eminent as a Christian, and an instrument for good, as he had been eminent in sin, and an instrument for evil.

In later years he looked back at her faith and thanked the Lord for the answer.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE ASKED IF SHE BELIEVED HE WOULD EVER BE CONVERTED. SHE SAID HE WOULD BE AS EMINENT FOR GOOD.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Mother's Prayers Answered."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 51:

"There be many that say, Who will shew us any good? But this we say, Lord, lift up the light of thy countenance upon us, and that shall put gladness into our hearts more than they have whose corn and wine increaseth." Psalm 4:6, 7.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: THERE BE MANY THAT SAY, WHO WILL SHEW US ANY GOOD?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 51. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A mother gave her two little ones books and toys and went upstairs. After half an hour a child called from the foot of the stairs, Mamma, are you there? The answer was, Yes, darling. The child said, All right, and went back to play. The question came again, and again the child went on.

The book sets beside that call the words, Fear not; I am with thee. I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. The first sentence is the opening of Isaiah 41:10. The second is Hebrews 13:5.
Alt text(s): Image reading: FEAR NOT; I AM WITH THEE. - As quoted in Wonders of Prayer
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Are You There."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A little boy and his mother were walking home from a visit. The night was very dark. She led him by the hand. He had only begun to remember the stories of the Bible, and he trusted what he heard.

After a silent walk he said, Mamma, I'm not afraid. She asked why. He said, Because, mamma, God keeps hold of the other hand.

The same bank entry then turns into a general lesson.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE NIGHT WAS DARK. HE SAID HE WAS NOT AFRAID, BECAUSE GOD KEPT HOLD OF THE OTHER HAND.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("God Keeps Hold Of The Other Hand."). Retold here in modern English.

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 36.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OF OLD HAST THOU LAID THE FOUNDATION OF THE EARTH
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 36.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 228:

"The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord. Shall we receive good at the hand of the Lord, and shall we not receive evil also?" Job 1:21. Job 2:10.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: SHALL WE RECEIVE GOOD AT THE HAND OF THE LORD, AND SHALL WE NOT RECEIVE EVIL ALSO?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 228. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A lady and a gentleman were walking up Madison Avenue from church. She said they were getting up Christmas decorations and an entertainment for their mission school. He told her to put his name down for anything she liked, and a sum came to his mind. A note reminded him. He sent the sum he had first thought of, twenty-five dollars.

The next Sabbath she said the gift was too large and she would give part back. He would not take it. She took fifteen dollars from her muff and forced it into his hand. He had meant it for the Lord.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE GAVE TWENTY-FIVE FOR THE MISSION SCHOOL. SHE TOOK FIFTEEN FROM HER MUFF AND FORCED IT BACK.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("That Beautiful Christmas Gift. How the Lord Used it."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
The New York Observer told of United States and railroad bonds and mortgages, one hundred and sixty thousand dollars, stolen on February 16, 1877, from the banking house of James G. King's Sons. They belonged to Edgar H. Richards. No clue held. Richards said he had never lost faith that prayer would bring the property back.

A stranger told Elliott F. Shepard, one of King's counsel, that he could get the treasure. At the hour, a little boy delivered an ordinary pasteboard bandbox wrapped in newspaper. He had come in a pelting rain. The paper tore and showed a blue hat box. A gentleman had given the boy a dime to bring it. Richards and a clerk checked the contents and found every missing item. The same entry then turns to Moody as a boy.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: ON FEBRUARY 16, 1877, BONDS OF ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY THOUSAND WERE STOLEN. A BOY BROUGHT A BANDBOX IN THE RAIN.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Stolen Bonds Returned."). Retold here in modern English.

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 37.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: O GOD, THOU HAST SEARCHED US AND KNOWN US
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 37.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Prof. Hitchcock's illustration, as the Cyclopaedia prints it, is the mineral called hydrophanous, a variety of opal. It is not transparent until it is immersed in water. He says it is so with many a Christian: until the floods of adversity have been poured over him, the character looks clouded, and trials give it distinctness.

No person is named beyond the professor who makes it.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SOME MINERALS ARE NOT CLEAR UNTIL THEY ARE PUT IN WATER. SO, HE SAYS, WITH MANY A CHRISTIAN.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Adversity, Influence of, Prof. Hitchcock").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 35:

"Who can utter the mighty acts of the Lord, who can shew forth all his praise?" Psalm 106:2.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHO CAN UTTER THE MIGHTY ACTS OF THE LORD, WHO CAN SHEW FORTH ALL HIS PRAISE?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 35. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
The Cyclopaedia tells of two boys, Augustus and Eugene, playing with one top, spinning it by turns. They grew angry. Eugene said it was his turn. Augustus said, You lie. They seized each other. Eugene took a sharp knife from his pocket and stabbed Augustus, who died in a few moments.

The book says one lost his life and the other became a murderer, over whose turn it was to spin a top.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: TWO BOYS HAD ONE TOP. EUGENE SAID IT WAS HIS TURN. IN THE SCUFFLE AUGUSTUS WAS STABBED.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Anger, two boys and a top").

Text:
Mr. Wesley records, as the Cyclopaedia gives it, that when he was enabled to believe in Christ under the reading of Luther's Preface to the Epistle to the Romans, at about a quarter before nine, in Aldersgate Street, he felt his heart strangely warmed. He felt he did trust in Christ alone for salvation, and that assurance was given him that Jesus had taken away his sins and saved him from the law of sin and death.

The hour, the street, and the warmed heart are clear.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: ABOUT A QUARTER BEFORE NINE, IN ALDERSGATE STREET, HIS HEART WAS STRANGELY WARMED.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Assurance, Wesley at Aldersgate").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 38.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: WE KNOW, O GOD, THAT THOU CANST DO EVERY THING
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 38.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Dr. Stebbing of Gray's Inn, in a sermon on Hume and some other metaphysical writers, said the thoughts went back to the author of the first philosophy, who likewise engaged to open the eyes of the public. He did so. The only discovery they found themselves able to make was that they were naked.

The Cyclopaedia gives that comparison and no further story.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE SAID THEY OPENED THE EYES OF THE PUBLIC. THE ONLY DISCOVERY WAS THAT THEY WERE NAKED.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Atheism, Dr. Stebbing on Hume").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 73:

"And what are we profited, if we should gain the whole world, and lose our own souls?" Matthew 16:26.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHAT ARE WE PROFITED, IF WE SHOULD GAIN THE WHOLE WORLD, AND LOSE OUR OWN SOULS?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 73. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: The Cyclopaedia, under Jesus, prints his proclamation: Come unto me, all ye that labor, and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. It adds that he demonstrated his compassion by dying for us.
Alt text(s): Image reading: COME UNTO ME, ALL YE THAT LABOR. - Matthew 11:28
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Jesus. Come unto me."). Retold here in modern English.

Text: ''Clergymen were talking of their success in preaching. One said, Gentlemen, I once converted a man with my eyes. A straggler entered the church and thought the preacher was staring at him. He moved from door to door to get out of that look. It did not help. He resolved to stare the preacher out of countenance. His attention was fixed on what was said, and from that day his sentiments and conduct changed.''
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE SAID HE ONCE CONVERTED A MAN WITH HIS EYES. THE MAN MOVED FROM DOOR TO DOOR AND THEN LISTENED.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Attention, the straggler").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 39.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: THOU HAST PROCLAIMED THY NAME
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 39.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 73:

"What fruit have we now in those things whereof we have cause to be ashamed; seeing the end of those things is death?" Romans 6:21.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHAT FRUIT HAVE WE NOW IN THOSE THINGS WHEREOF WE HAVE CAUSE TO BE ASHAMED; SEEING THE END OF THOSE THINGS IS DEATH?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 73. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A brother said that when he was young in the service of God he feared he would backslide if he lived to old age. He sometimes asked to die young, so religion would not be reproached and his soul would not be ruined.

One day the impression was made that he must serve God by the day. He said this was more than thirty years ago, and that by grace to keep that rule he was still on the way.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE HAD ASKED TO DIE YOUNG, LEST HE BACKSLIDE. THE WORD THAT CAME WAS, SERVE GOD BY THE DAY.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Backsliding, serve God by the day").

Text:
A Christian who had made heavy losses was asked by his pastor about the missionary collection. The pastor said he had already made it, and, knowing the loss, had not thought it proper to call for the usual donation.

The man answered that he had suffered great losses and must be prudent, but retrenchment must not begin at the house of God.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE HAD SUFFERED GREAT LOSSES. HE SAID RETRENCHMENT MUST NOT BEGIN AT THE HOUSE OF GOD.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Beneficence, no retrenchment").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 42.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: THOU ART THE MOST HIGH, WHO RULEST IN THE KINGDOM OF MEN,
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 42.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Mr. Newton of London said to a gentleman who had lately lost a daughter: if you were going to the East Indies, you would like to send a remittance before you. This little girl is like a remittance sent to heaven before you.

He added that a merchant is not heard grieving that his ship has got into port so soon, and has escaped the storms that are coming. Neither, he said, should we sorrow over children dying. The figure of the ship and the remittance is clear.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: NEWTON SAID THE CHILD WAS LIKE A REMITTANCE SENT AHEAD. A MERCHANT DOES NOT GRIEVE THAT THE SHIP IS IN PORT.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Bereavement, Newton and the ship").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 71:

"We have lost our first love, and where is now the blessedness we sometimes spake of?" Revelation 2:4. Galatians 4:15.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WE HAVE LOST OUR FIRST LOVE, AND WHERE IS NOW THE BLESSEDNESS WE SOMETIMES SPAKE OF?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 71. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Bernard Gilpin, accused of heresy before Bishop Bonner, set out for London. His maxim was, All things are for the best. On the journey he broke his leg. A companion asked, in scorn, whether all was for the best now. Gilpin said he still believed so.

Before he could resume the journey, Queen Mary died. Instead of going to London to be burned, he returned home.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: GILPIN, SENT TO LONDON BEFORE BONNER, BROKE HIS LEG. BEFORE HE COULD GO ON, QUEEN MARY DIED.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Best, Bernard Gilpin").

Text:
The Rev. W. Romaine, asked to play at cards, made no objection. When the cards were produced he said, Let us ask the blessing of God. The lady exclaimed that she had never heard of asking God's blessing on a game of cards.

Romaine replied, Ought we to engage in anything on which we cannot ask his blessing?
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THEY ASKED ROMAINE TO PLAY AT CARDS. HE SAID, LET US ASK THE BLESSING OF GOD.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Cards, William Romaine").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 43.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: AND SINCE IT IS THE WILL OF GOD
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 43.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
The wife of a petty official in New York called on her daughter's teacher to ask what progress the girl was making. He said she was doing as well as could be expected, and only wanted a capacity.

The mother said he should have told them before, since her father was able to buy her one.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE ASKED HOW HER DAUGHTER WAS DOING. HE SAID THE GIRL ONLY WANTED A CAPACITY. THE MOTHER SAID HER FATHER COULD BUY ONE.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Capacity, the New York mother").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 125:

"We will praise thee, for we are fearfully and wonderfully made, and that our souls, our nobler part, know right well; for what man knows the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him?" Psalm 139:14. 1 Corinthians 2:11.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHAT MAN KNOWS THE THINGS OF A MAN, SAVE THE SPIRIT OF MAN WHICH IS IN HIM?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 125. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: The Cyclopaedia, under Christ, prints the words, I am the Way, and says a road is that along which men go to their daily work, which is why the figure is used.
Alt text(s): Image reading: I AM THE WAY. - John 14:6
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Christ. I am the Way."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A little boy told his parents he should like to have lived in the time of the Saviour, so he might have done something for him. His mother asked, smiling, what a child of his age could have done to prove his good will.

He reflected an instant and said he would have run everywhere, doing his errands.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE WISHED HE HAD LIVED WHEN THE SAVIOUR DID, SO HE COULD DO SOMETHING. HE SAID HE WOULD HAVE RUN HIS ERRANDS.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Child, errands for the Saviour").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 44.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: THOU, LORD, ART THE FORMER OF OUR BODIES
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 44.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 127:

"It may be we were sent forth without purse or scrip, but lacked we any thing? Nothing, Lord." Luke 22:35.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: IT MAY BE WE WERE SENT FORTH WITHOUT PURSE OR SCRIP, BUT LACKED WE ANY THING?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 127. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A young prince, whose mind had begun to value religious truth, asked his tutor for instruction so he might be prepared for death. The tutor said there was plenty of time when he was older.

The prince said no. He had been to the churchyard and measured the graves, and there were many shorter than he was.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HIS TUTOR SAID THERE WAS PLENTY OF TIME WHEN HE WAS OLDER. HE HAD MEASURED THE GRAVES. MANY WERE SHORTER THAN HE.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Children, the short graves").

Text:
A rich Campanian lady, fond of show, visited Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, and displayed her diamonds. She asked to see Cornelia's jewels also.

Cornelia turned the talk until her sons came back from the public schools. When they entered she pointed to them and said, These are my jewels, the only ornaments I admire.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE ASKED TO SEE CORNELIA'S JEWELS. THE SONS CAME IN FROM SCHOOL. CORNELIA SAID, THESE ARE MY JEWELS.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Children, Cornelia's jewels").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 45.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: THOU ART THE GOD THAT HAST FED US ALL OUR LIFE LONG
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 45.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A child who had a mother asked a child who had none what he did without a mother to tell his troubles to. The orphan said his mother had told him whom to go to before she died. He went to the Lord Jesus. He was mother's friend, and he was his.

The other child said Jesus was away off, with many things to attend to, and was not likely to stop for him. The orphan said he did not know about that. All he knew was that Jesus says he will, and that was enough.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE ASKED WHAT THE ORPHAN DID WITHOUT A MOTHER TO TELL. HE SAID HIS MOTHER HAD TOLD HIM WHOM TO GO TO.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Christ a friend, the orphan").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 142:

"And hath God by his grace translated us out of the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom of his dear Son?" Colossians 1:13.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: HATH GOD BY HIS GRACE TRANSLATED US OUT OF THE KINGDOM OF DARKNESS INTO THE KINGDOM OF HIS DEAR SON?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 142. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A voyager had been storm-tossed for several days on a dangerous coast. As the ship was about to pass a point of greater danger, he hesitated to go to his stateroom, lest the sailors fail through weariness and the ship be wrecked. He told the captain his fear.

The captain said he need not fear: I shall stand at the helm. The book sets that word beside Jesus and the timid soul.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE SHIP WAS ABOUT TO PASS A WORSE POINT. HE FEARED THE SAILORS WERE WORN OUT. THE CAPTAIN SAID, I SHALL STAND AT THE HELM.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Christ at the helm").

Text:
Wolfe, being wounded, laid himself on the ground. A shout came. An officer near him exclaimed that they ran. The dying man asked who ran. The officer said the enemy, and that they gave way everywhere.

Wolfe said, Now God be praised: I shall die happy. He turned on his side and died. This is a death in battle, not a cure.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: WOLFE, WOUNDED, LAY ON THE GROUND. A SHOUT. THEY RUN, THE OFFICER SAID. WOLFE ANSWERED, NOW GOD BE PRAISED: I SHALL DIE HAPPY.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Wolfe at Quebec").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 46.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: THOU ART OUR KING, O GOD
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 46.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A girl of thirteen found her Saviour and told her mother. The mother, in tears, said God had heard her prayers. She had expected the conversion at thirteen.

The girl said she had often felt like submitting when she was only four or five. The mother said she had not expected it then. She was only sowing the seed. She had not expected a Christian until the girl was thirteen.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE WAS THIRTEEN WHEN SHE FOUND THE SAVIOUR. HER MOTHER SAID, I WAS ONLY SOWING THE SEED.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Early conversions, thirteen").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 35:

"Who is a God like unto thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?" Exodus 15:11.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHO IS A GOD LIKE UNTO THEE, GLORIOUS IN HOLINESS, FEARFUL IN PRAISES, DOING WONDERS?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 35. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
The section headed His Covenant is a chain of promises, not an incident. One sentence it prints is, He is faithful that promised.

The words are those of Hebrews 10:23.
Alt text(s): Image reading: HE IS FAITHFUL THAT PROMISED. - As printed in Wonders of Prayer
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("His Covenant."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A young colored soldier threw away a piece of hardtack. Another soldier said he ought not to do that, and asked if he had forgotten Fair Oaks so soon.

Remembering the three days in which they nearly starved, the young soldier gathered up the fragments and put them in his haversack.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE THREW AWAY A PIECE OF HARDTACK. THE OTHER SAID, HAVE YOU FORGOT FAIR OAKS SO SOON?
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Economy, Fair Oaks").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 47.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: THOU HAST DIRECTED US TO ASK AND SEEK AND KNOCK
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 47.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 94:

"Hast thou but one blessing? Yea, thou hast many blessings: Bless us, even us also, O our Father; yea, let the blessing of Abraham come upon us, which comes upon the Gentiles through faith." Genesis 27:38. Galatians 3:14.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: HAST THOU BUT ONE BLESSING?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 94. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: At the rupture of the Peace of Amiens, Napoleon said to Lord Whitworth, I will make an attack on England. Whitworth answered, That is your affair, sir. Napoleon said he would annihilate them. Whitworth answered, Ah, sir, that is our affair.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: NAPOLEON SAID HE WOULD ATTACK ENGLAND. WHITWORTH ANSWERED, THAT IS YOUR AFFAIR. THEN, OF ANNIHILATION, THAT IS OURS.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Endurance, Whitworth and Napoleon").

Text:
An eminent minister, silent in company for a considerable time, was asked the reason. He said the powers of his mind had been absorbed with everlasting happiness.

He said, Oh my friends, consider what it is to be forever with the Lord, forever, forever, forever.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE HAD BEEN SILENT. THEY ASKED WHY. HE SAID, CONSIDER WHAT IT IS TO BE FOREVER WITH THE LORD.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Eternity, forever with the Lord").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 54.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: WE COME IN THE NAME OF THE GREAT HIGH PRIEST
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 54.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: The Cyclopaedia says there is a parish in Savoy with this placard in every house: Understand well the force of the words, A God, a moment, an eternity. A God who sees thee, a moment which flees from thee, an eternity which awaits thee.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: A PARISH IN SAVOY, THE BOOK SAYS, PUTS IN EVERY HOUSE THE WORDS A GOD, A MOMENT, AN ETERNITY.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Eternity, the Savoy placard").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 65:

"Our hearts are deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked; who can know them?" Jeremiah 17:9.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: OUR HEARTS ARE DECEITFUL ABOVE ALL THINGS, AND DESPERATELY WICKED; WHO CAN KNOW THEM?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 65. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A teacher of the freedmen in a Southern state sat at a window and watched two men loading goods into a cart. One was disposed to shirk. The other stopped, looked at him, and asked, Sam, do you expect to go to heaven?

Sam said yes. The other said, Then take hold and lift.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: ONE WAS SHIRKING THE LOAD. THE OTHER ASKED IF HE EXPECTED TO GO TO HEAVEN. THEN, TAKE HOLD AND LIFT.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Expectation, take hold and lift").

Text:
A poor widow was weeping in the room where her husband's body lay. Their only child came in and asked why she wept so. She told him of their loss, and especially of their poverty.

The child looked into her face and said, Is God dead, mother?
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE WEPT WHERE HER HUSBAND LAY. THE CHILD ASKED WHY, AND SHE SPOKE OF THEIR POVERTY. HE SAID, IS GOD DEAD?
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Faith, is God dead").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 61.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: BUT THERE IS FORGIVENESS WITH THEE THAT THOU MAYEST BE FEARED
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 61.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: When Sidney was told he might save his life by a falsehood, by denying his handwriting, he answered that when God has brought a man to a dilemma where he must assert a lie or lose his life, God gives a clear indication of duty, which is to prefer death to falsehood.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE WAS TOLD HE MIGHT LIVE IF HE DENIED HIS HAND. HE SAID GOD HAD SHOWN HIM TO PREFER DEATH TO FALSEHOOD.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Falsehood, Algernon Sidney").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 91:

"Hast thou not appointed that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in Christ’s name unto all nations?" Luke 24:47.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: HAST THOU NOT APPOINTED THAT REPENTANCE AND REMISSION OF SINS SHOULD BE PREACHED IN CHRIST’S NAME UNTO ALL NATIONS?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 91. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Another sentence in His Covenant is, I will not suffer my faithfulness to fail. The section gives the promise and no incident.

The words are those of Psalm 89:33.
Alt text(s): Image reading: I WILL NOT SUFFER MY FAITHFULNESS TO FAIL. - As printed in Wonders of Prayer
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("His Covenant."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
The Cyclopaedia records that when Anaximander was told the very boys laughed at his singing, he said, Then I must learn to sing better.

The same entry has other sayings of Epictetus and Plato.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE BOYS LAUGHED AT HIS SINGING. ANAXIMANDER SAID, THEN I MUST LEARN TO SING BETTER.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Calumny, Anaximander").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 66.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: WE HAVE KNOWN TO DO GOOD, BUT HAVE NOT DONE IT
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 66.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 68:

"Who can understand his errors? Cleanse thou us from secret faults." Psalm 19:12.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHO CAN UNDERSTAND HIS ERRORS?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 68. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Plato, being told that he had many enemies who spoke ill of him, said it was no matter. He would live so that none would believe them.

Hearing at another time that an intimate friend had spoken detractingly of him, he said he was sure the friend would not have done it if he had not some reason.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE WAS TOLD HE HAD MANY ENEMIES. PLATO SAID IT WAS NO MATTER. HE WOULD LIVE SO THAT NONE WOULD BELIEVE THEM.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Calumny, Plato").

Text:
The Cyclopaedia relates of King Oswald that he was sitting at dinner on Easter Day, a silver dish of dainty meats before him. They were about to bless the bread when his almoner came in and said poor hungry people were at the door, begging food.

He ordered the dish of meat carried out to them, and the dish itself cut in pieces and divided among them.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: IT WAS EASTER DAY. THE POOR WERE AT THE DOOR. OSWALD SENT OUT THE SILVER DISH AND HAD IT CUT IN PIECES.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Charity, King Oswald").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 69.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: WE HAVE BEEN SOON ANGRY, AND ANGER HATH RESTED IN OUR BOSOMS.
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 69.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
The Indians to whom Columbus first applied for provisions refused them. Foreseeing an eclipse, he threatened sudden destruction, and as a sign said the sun would be darkened within two days.

When the eclipse came they were filled with fear and brought large supplies. The book says they gave, but it was not charity.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THEY REFUSED HIM PROVISIONS. HE TOLD THEM THE SUN WOULD DARKEN. WHEN IT DID, THEY BROUGHT LARGE SUPPLIES.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Charity, Columbus and the eclipse").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 47:

"For should not a people seek unto their God? Whither shall we go but to thee? Thou hast the words of eternal life." Isaiah 8:19. John 6:68.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHITHER SHALL WE GO BUT TO THEE?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 47. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
It is said of the German schoolmaster John Trebonius, instructor of Martin Luther, that he always appeared before his boys with uncovered head. Who can tell, he said, what may yet rise up amid these youths? There may be learned doctors, sage legislators, nay, princes of the empire.

The book adds that even then the solitary monk who shook the world was among them.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE CAME BEFORE HIS BOYS WITH HIS HEAD UNCOVERED. WHO CAN TELL, HE SAID, WHAT MAY YET RISE UP AMONG THEM?
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Children, Trebonius").

Text:
A party of children were amusing themselves with a bird. They had fastened a string to its leg. It fluttered into the air and wished to escape, then was suddenly checked and drawn downward.

Gotthold, who saw it, thought it was so with the soul entangled with temporal things.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: CHILDREN HAD TIED A STRING TO A BIRD'S LEG. IT ROSE AND WAS PULLED BACK DOWN.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Cares, Gotthold and the bird").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 70.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR FRETFULNESS AND IMPATIENCE AND MURMURING UNDER OUR AFFLICTIONS, OUR INORDINATE DEJECTION,
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 70.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
During a session of Congress, Jefferson pointed out Roger Sherman to a friend and said, That is Mr. Sherman of Connecticut, a man who never said a foolish thing in his life.

Mr. Macon said Sherman had more common sense than any man he ever knew. Fisher Ames said that if he was absent from a discussion and did not know how to vote, he looked at Roger Sherman, sure that a vote with him would be right. The book adds that Sherman was faithful in his closet, his family, on the bench, and in the senate.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: JEFFERSON POINTED AND SAID, THAT IS MR. SHERMAN, A MAN WHO NEVER SAID A FOOLISH THING.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Character, Roger Sherman").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 240:

"Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire besides thee."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHOM HAVE I IN HEAVEN BUT THEE?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 240. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
His Covenant also prints, The word of our God shall stand forever. There is no story with it.

The words are those of Isaiah 40:8.
Alt text(s): Image reading: THE WORD OF OUR GOD SHALL STAND FOREVER. - As printed in Wonders of Prayer
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("His Covenant."). Retold here in modern English.

Text: The writer once visited the Rajah of Burdwan and found him sitting in his treasury. Fifty bags, each containing a thousand rupees, five hundred dollars, were before him. Asked what he was doing with the money, the rajah said it was for his god.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: FIFTY BAGS STOOD BEFORE THE RAJAH. EACH HELD A THOUSAND RUPEES. HE SAID, IT IS FOR MY GOD.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Charity, the Rajah of Burdwan").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 72.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: AND THAT WHICH IS AT THE BOTTOM OF ALL
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 72.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 90:

"It is God that justifieth, who is he that shall condemn? It is Christ that died, yea rather that is risen again, and now is even at the right hand of God; who also maketh intercession for us, and whose blood speaks better things than that of Abel." Romans 8:33, 34. Hebrews 12:24.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: IT IS GOD THAT JUSTIFIETH, WHO IS HE THAT SHALL CONDEMN?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 90. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A little Massachusetts boy, about two, was playing with knitting needles. His mother passed through and said he must not lose them. They were not his needles. They were hers.

As she left she heard him saying he must not lose them, they were not his, and if he lost them he would be despised, and when he grew up people would look at him and ask where those needles were.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE WAS ABOUT TWO. HIS MOTHER SAID THE NEEDLES WERE HERS. HE REPEATED THAT IF HE LOST THEM HE WOULD BE DESPISED.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Children, the knitting needles").

Text:
A king once said to a favorite, Ask what thou wilt, and I will give it. The man thought that if he asked to be a general he would obtain it, and if he asked half the kingdom it would be given. He would ask for something to which all these things would be added.

He said, Give me thy daughter to wife. The book says this made him heir to the wealth and honors of the kingdom, and sets the choice beside choosing Christ.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE KING SAID, ASK WHAT THOU WILT. THE FAVORITE ASKED FOR THE DAUGHTER, AND WITH HER THE REST.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Choice, the king's daughter").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 77.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: WE DID, AND YET WE HAVE RETURNED
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 77.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A clergyman said that soon after he dedicated himself to Christ he resolved, as Jacob did, Of all that thou shalt give me, I will surely give a tenth unto thee. Of the first five hundred dollars he earned, he gave one hundred and thirty, in such a way that a wealthy friend gave several hundreds more, including one hundred dollars to the clergyman.

For four years he said his expenses were small and the only luxury was the luxury of giving. In the first two of those years he gave five hundred dollars. Over about sixteen years he gave nearly twelve hundred, creating about forty life memberships. He said his congregation had given more in those sixteen years than in all their previous history.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: OF THE FIRST FIVE HUNDRED DOLLARS HE EARNED, HE GAVE A HUNDRED AND THIRTY, AFTER JACOB'S TENTH.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("It Pays To Give To The Lord."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 69:

"When we did eat, and when we did drink, did we not eat to ourselves, and drink to ourselves?" Zechariah 7:6.
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHEN WE DID EAT, AND WHEN WE DID DRINK, DID WE NOT EAT TO OURSELVES, AND DRINK TO OURSELVES?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 69. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
In New Haven lived a widow, almost helpless, with no money and only a temporary home from acquaintances. She had prayed and received nothing this time. The parties had never known each other.

A man received her note. No money was asked. The words came to him, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto the least of these, my children, ye have done it unto me. He wrote a check for twenty-five dollars and said he did not know her need. He later feared he had misdirected the letter and sent a postal card telling her to ask at the post office. She had the card and not the letter. The letter was at the office.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE HAD NOT ASKED HIM FOR MONEY. HE SENT TWENTY-FIVE, THEN A CARD, BECAUSE HE FEARED THE LETTER WAS MISDIRECTED.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("That Wonderful $25. Another Evidence of the Ever-Present Spirit of God."). Retold here in modern English.

Text: Some time ago, the Cyclopaedia says, half a dozen young men dressed in green were shooting at a target with bows and arrows. The arrows of one invariably struck the earth, because he aimed too low. Someone cried, Aim higher.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HALF A DOZEN YOUNG MEN IN GREEN SHOT AT A TARGET. ONE MAN'S ARROWS STRUCK THE EARTH. SOMEONE CRIED, AIM HIGHER.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Aim, aim higher").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 78.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: WE KNOW THAT THE LAW CURSETH EVERY ONE
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 78.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: You are the first of your line, an opponent sneered at Cicero. He answered, And you are the last of yours.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: AN OPPONENT SNEERED THAT CICERO WAS THE FIRST OF HIS LINE. HE ANSWERED, AND YOU ARE THE LAST OF YOURS.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Ancestry, Cicero").

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 257:

"Go along with us to the solemn assembly; for if thy presence go not up with us, wherefore should we go up?"
Alt text(s): Question card reading: IF THY PRESENCE GO NOT UP WITH US, WHEREFORE SHOULD WE GO UP?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 257. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A dying Christian soldier asked the nurse for two cups of water, one for himself and one for his friend, who, he said, had come a long distance and must be tired.

The nurse, startled, said, I don't see anybody. This is a deathbed, not a cure.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE DYING SOLDIER ASKED FOR TWO CUPS OF WATER, ONE FOR HIMSELF AND ONE FOR THE FRIEND THE NURSE COULD NOT SEE.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Angel, the two cups").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 81.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: WE HAVE HEARD OF THEE BY THE HEARING OF THE EAR
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 81.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 222:

"What would we that thou shouldest do for us? This is our hearts desire and prayer in the first place, Father in heaven, let thy name be sanctified."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: WHAT WOULD WE THAT THOU SHOULDEST DO FOR US?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 222. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
After Sabat, an Arabian who had professed faith through the labors of the Rev. H. Martyn, had turned back and written for Mohammedanism, he was met at Malacca by the Rev. Dr. Milne. Milne put pointed questions. Sabat said, I am unhappy. I have a mountain of burning sand on my head. When I go about, I know not what I am doing.

The book adds that it is an evil thing and bitter to forsake the Lord.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: AFTER HE TURNED BACK, SABAT MET DR. MILNE AT MALACCA. HE SAID, I HAVE A MOUNTAIN OF BURNING SAND ON MY HEAD.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Backslider, Sabat").

Text:
John Newton, asked, Are you a Calvinist? said he was more of a Calvinist than anything else, but he used his Calvinism in writing and preaching as he did a piece of sugar. He took a lump, put it into his teacup, and stirred it. He said he did not give it alone and whole, but mixed and diluted.

He hoped he was, on the whole, a scriptural preacher, for he was considered an Arminian among the Calvinists and a Calvinist among the strenuous Arminians.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: ASKED IF HE WAS A CALVINIST, NEWTON TOOK A LUMP OF SUGAR, PUT IT IN HIS CUP, AND SAID HE DID NOT GIVE IT ALONE AND WHOLE.
Comment(s): Source: New Cyclopaedia of Prose Illustrations (1875), public domain ("Calvinism, Newton's sugar").

Text: This is Matthew Henry's sentence, from A Method for Prayer, page 91.
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: AND AS FAR AS THE EAST IS FROM THE WEST
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer, page 91.. Public domain. Quoted word for word.
